article.title: Ethical Problems of Corporations

abstract.para: A discussion of why corporations are a bad idea from an ethical standpoint. These problems are specific to corporations and do not apply to other forms of business organization such as partnerships.

article.para: Publicly held corporations have a hard time being ethical. The problem is that their entire structure prevents the possibility of ethical action.

To be ethical, someone, somewhere must be able to make an ethical choice. Who would that be in a publicly-held corporation? Could that be the board of directors? Actually, their hands are pretty tied. In order to be on the board of directors, you have to have one goal in mind - shareholder equity. Any other consideration just goes out the door. If someone on the board were to suggest that a plan, while profitable, would be ethically questionable, they would be removed from the board, or simply laughed at. So, since the board isn't going to give ethical direction, the shareholders must be the ones to pin the responsibility on for ethical decisions. However, the shareholders often know little about what decisions are even being made in the board room. Public companies still have many secrets that their shareholders aren't allowed to see. They also know little about the ethical quality of the people who are going to be on the board. In fact, most shareholders don't know enough to even vote.

Corporations face an additional ethical dilemma. Incorporating a business means that the only ones responsible for paying back corporate loans is the corporation. Therefore, if the corporation goes bankrupt, there is no longer anyone responsible for the money that is due. This has two implications. The first one is that, ethically, corporations who owe money are ethically bound to make smart business choices in order to survive long enough to pay back their debt. If those smart business practices are unethical, then they have to choose between being an unethical business, or not paying back their debt, which is also unethical. Secondly, by law corporations must put profits before ethics because of the corporation's responsibilities to its shareholders and debtors.

Corporations are powerless to make ethical choices because of their legal obligations to both their investors and creditors, and because there is no person or group of people to fulfill those obligations should the company cease being able to operate. In comparison, in a sole proprietorship or partnership, the owners are free to make ethical choices, because if the company fails they still have to pay their obligations. Therefore, although the moral road may be harder, they have the ability to make the proper choices.
